title: Jackson Hole: Exploring the Financial Frontier - Liberty Street Economics
gist: NY Fed research head Kartik B. Athreya reports that the 2026 Jackson Hole symposium's main theme was payments innovation — blockchain rails that let parties pay each other without a central hub. He frames the core risk as stablecoin runs and deposit flight hollowing out the information banks need to allocate credit, and flags Todd Keister's narrow-banking work and Pablo Azar's research on crypto-collateralized stablecoins as the NY Fed's response.

insights.claim: The 2026 Kansas City Fed Jackson Hole symposium made financial innovation in the payments space its main theme, shifting the marquee central-bank gathering away from rates and inflation toward payment rails and market structure.
insights.speaker: Kartik B. Athreya
insights.so_what: The Fed's top policy forum is now allocating agenda time to payments plumbing — a leading indicator of where regulatory attention and rulemaking energy will go next.
insights.quote: The main theme of this year’s Kansas City Fed symposium was financial innovation in the payments space—a fast-evolving topic with major implications for consumers and central bankers alike.
insights.locator: Intro: 'After two days of heady discussions'

insights.claim: Jackson Hole discussion centered on technologies that let payments be made directly between parties without a traditional coordinating hub, the role central banks have long filled by providing the hub and the payment 'rails'.
insights.speaker: Kartik B. Athreya
insights.so_what: The incumbent being disintermediated here is the central bank itself as operator of payment rails; watch for defensive Fed initiatives on settlement infrastructure.
insights.locator: Econ in the Tetons: 'Much of the conversation at Jackson Hole'

insights.claim: The New York Fed frames its interest in payment innovation around three self-interested questions: how the changes should be supported, what to expect as a payments processor itself, and what risks they pose to the payments and financial systems.
insights.speaker: Kartik B. Athreya
insights.so_what: Tells you the lens supervisors will apply to any new payment venture — support, own-franchise impact, and systemic risk, in that order.
insights.locator: Econ in the Tetons: 'So naturally, we at the Fed are interested'

insights.claim: Papers presented at the symposium were split, with some welcoming blockchain-enabled smart contracts and others taking a cautionary line on the implications for banks, non-bank financial institutions, and consumer well-being.
insights.speaker: Kartik B. Athreya
insights.so_what: The official research community has not converged on a verdict, so regulatory outcomes on tokenized payments remain genuinely two-sided rather than pre-decided.
insights.quote: some of the papers presented were more cautionary in assessing the implications of such innovations for both banks and other entities who do “bank-like” things
insights.locator: Econ in the Tetons: 'Conference participants demonstrated'

insights.claim: Blockchain's clearest accepted benefit is smart contracts — richer payment arrangements made contingent on circumstances relevant to the paying parties — rather than speed or cost alone.
insights.speaker: Kartik B. Athreya
insights.so_what: Contingent, state-dependent payment logic is the feature policymakers concede is genuinely new; business models built on that have a better regulatory reception than pure cost-cutting pitches.
insights.locator: Econ in the Tetons: 'Conference participants demonstrated how some aspects'

insights.claim: The stated purpose of the financial system is to let economic participants concentrate purchasing power on desired goods and services at specific times and under specific circumstances, and all borrowing, lending, and insurance contracts exist to facilitate that.
insights.speaker: Kartik B. Athreya
insights.so_what: A first-principles test to apply to any fintech or crypto pitch: if it doesn't move purchasing power across time and states of the world, it isn't finance, it's plumbing.
insights.locator: From Basic Banking…: 'it’s useful to recall the basic purpose'

insights.claim: Every desired function of the financial system — including funding innovation via loans, venture capital, and equity issuance — ultimately depends on payment systems for delivery, so a financial system with weak payments is not fully delivering for society.
insights.speaker: Kartik B. Athreya
insights.so_what: Payments quality is upstream of capital formation; degradation in payment rails transmits directly into the cost and availability of risk capital.
insights.quote: Vitally, every single one of these desired functions relies in the end on payment systems for their delivery.
insights.locator: From Basic Banking…: 'Vitally, every single one'

insights.claim: Banks and, increasingly, non-bank financial institutions accumulate information on credit risk, economic conditions, and markets as a by-product of gathering deposits and lending, and that informational vantage is what lets them direct credit where it is most needed.
insights.speaker: Kartik B. Athreya
insights.so_what: The credit-allocation value of banks is informational, not balance-sheet — so anything that separates deposits from lending degrades information, not just funding.
insights.locator: From Basic Banking…: 'As intermediators, these institutions naturally amass'

insights.claim: Payments are treated as a natural adjunct to lending rather than a standalone business, because two customers of the same bank or NBFI can settle internally and networks exist to move claims between institutions.
insights.speaker: Kartik B. Athreya
insights.so_what: Unbundling payments from intermediation is the structural break blockchain enables; the Fed's framing implies it would be treated as a departure from the norm, not an efficiency.
insights.locator: From Basic Banking…: 'Payments are a natural adjunct'

insights.claim: Blockchain-based banking with distributed digital ledgers and tokenized deposits replacing traditional databases is presented as offering real-time transactions, higher security, and lower operational costs, but these are attributed to advocates rather than endorsed.
insights.speaker: Kartik B. Athreya
insights.so_what: Note the hedge: the NY Fed's research head reports the benefit case as claimed, not established — expect proof-of-benefit burdens in future policy work.
insights.quote: Advocates say that blockchain-based banking could offer a variety of benefits, most notably real-time transactions, higher security, and lower operational costs.
insights.locator: …To the Blockchain: 'Blockchain technology has the potential'

insights.claim: A large volume of information is currently exchanged before payments are effected and finalized, and the open question is how far emerging payment technologies can cut the time, effort, and resources those verification steps consume.
insights.speaker: Kartik B. Athreya
insights.so_what: Frames the real prize in payment tech as pre-settlement information cost, not transaction speed — a different set of winners than consumer-facing payment apps.
insights.locator: …To the Blockchain: 'The nature of the information needed'

insights.claim: Digital assets are subject to runs and shocks in the same way banks can be destabilized by depositor flight, according to documented New York Fed research.
insights.speaker: Kartik B. Athreya
insights.so_what: The run-equivalence framing is the analytical basis for eventually applying bank-style liquidity and reserve rules to stablecoin issuers.
insights.quote: Just as banks can be destabilized by depositor flight, our researchers have documented that digital assets can also be subject to runs and shocks.
insights.locator: Stablecoin Shocks?: 'Of course, the transition to blockchain-based banking'

insights.claim: Stablecoin adoption as a payment instrument has accelerated in recent years specifically because of the passage of the 2025 GENIUS Act.
insights.speaker: Kartik B. Athreya
insights.so_what: A named legislative catalyst dates the adoption inflection — useful for anchoring growth curves and for anticipating that the same legislature can decelerate it.
insights.quote: Stablecoins—blockchain-based crypto assets whose value is pegged to that of a fiat currency, usually the U.S. dollar—have seen rapid adoption as a payment instrument in recent years, accelerated by the passage of the 2025 GENIUS Act.
insights.locator: Stablecoin Shocks?: 'Stablecoins—blockchain-based crypto assets'

insights.claim: Despite a name implying a high degree of security, stablecoins are not fully immune from instability, and shocks to the stablecoin market have originated both from within the crypto industry and from traditional financial markets.
insights.speaker: Kartik B. Athreya
insights.so_what: Two independent shock channels mean stablecoin stress is not a crypto-only tail risk; traditional market stress can propagate into the peg.
insights.locator: Stablecoin Shocks?: 'Though their name implies'

insights.claim: A newer generation of stablecoins is pegged to other crypto assets rather than to a fiat currency such as the U.S. dollar, and New York Fed economist Pablo Azar and a coauthor argue this creates risks within the crypto ecosystem itself and thereby more broadly.
insights.speaker: Kartik B. Athreya
insights.so_what: Crypto-collateralized stablecoins reintroduce reflexive collateral loops the fiat-backed design removed; treat them as a distinct, higher-beta risk category from USD-backed issuers.
insights.locator: Systemic Effects: 'Instead of being linked to a traditional fiat currency'

insights.claim: The key systemic worry raised is that if households shift bank deposits into stablecoins, banks lose the capacity to gather the information and capital needed to lend to borrowers who need credit, with far-reaching reverberations.
insights.speaker: Kartik B. Athreya
insights.so_what: This is the transmission channel to watch: stablecoin AUM growth as a direct read on deposit-funded lending capacity and regional bank credit supply.
insights.quote: What if many of us simply shift our bank deposits into stablecoins, thus hampering banks’ capacity to gather the information and capital necessary to lend to those who need credit?
insights.locator: Systemic Effects: 'One practical example is the effect'

insights.claim: The wave of payment innovations has pushed economists back to a classic question — whether the same institution must both offer easy-to-withdraw deposits and issue hard-to-liquidate loans — with the New York Fed's Todd Keister examining a 'narrow bank' that provides payment and withdrawal services while leaving lending to finance companies.
insights.speaker: Kartik B. Athreya
insights.so_what: If narrow banking gains official intellectual support, the long-run structure splits payments franchises from credit franchises — a re-rating event for both bank and specialty-finance business models.
insights.locator: Systemic Effects: 'is it really essential for the same institution'

themes.theme: Two tests and the taxpayer backstop

insights.claim: Two tests are proposed for any new payment protocol, platform, or instrument: whether it enables transactions that were not feasible before or makes them cheaper, and how much it changes the risks facing all parties in the financial system and the broader economy.
insights.speaker: Kartik B. Athreya
insights.so_what: A concise screen for evaluating payment ventures the way their regulator will: novel-or-cheaper on one axis, risk transfer on the other.
insights.locator: Street Level Observations: 'it’s important to keep things in perspective'

insights.claim: The same properties that make stablecoins attractive for cheap cross-border payments and make tokenization of safe assets like U.S. Treasury securities attractive for tradability might create risks for incumbent payment providers, most obviously banks.
insights.speaker: Kartik B. Athreya
insights.so_what: Benefit and disruption are the same mechanism here; banks' payment revenue is the identified casualty of successful tokenization.
insights.locator: Street Level Observations: 'Stablecoins, for example, are typically promoted'

insights.claim: Because banking and payments are areas where taxpayer support has historically been used to stop problems from worsening, the priority for future work is avoiding the transference of risk from private innovators to the public.
insights.speaker: Kartik B. Athreya
insights.so_what: Signals that the regulatory test applied to stablecoin and tokenization firms will be implicit-backstop creep, not consumer protection alone — the binding constraint on how large these franchises can get.
insights.quote: more research and a sharp eye toward avoiding the transference of risks to the public are both going to be important
insights.locator: Street Level Observations: 'Moreover, both banking and payments'
